latin: EDWARD[US] REX
en: King Edward
note: Edward the Confessor, King of England, sits on his throne talking with two men, probably including Harold. The tapestry opens before anyone knows a crisis is coming. Historians think the word EDWARD was touched up by later restorers.

latin: UBI HAROLD DUX ANGLORUM ET SUI MILITES EQUITANT AD BOSHAM ECCLESIA[M]
en: Where Harold, an English leader, rides with his knights to the church at Bosham
note: Harold Godwinson, the most powerful earl in England, rides out with hounds and a hawk on his wrist and stops to pray at Bosham on the Sussex coast.

latin: HIC HAROLD MARE NAVIGAVIT
en: Here Harold sailed across the sea
note: Nobody is sure why Harold crossed the Channel. Norman writers said King Edward sent him to promise William the crown.

latin: ET VELIS VENTO PLENIS VENIT IN TERRA WIDONIS COMITIS
en: and with the wind filling his sails he came to the land of Count Guy
note: Harold lands in Ponthieu, the territory of Count Guy (Wido), on the French coast.

latin: HAROLD
en: Harold
note: Harold steps ashore, and things are about to go wrong for him.

latin: HIC APPREHENDIT WIDO HAROLDU[M]
en: Here Guy seizes Harold
note: Count Guy arrests Harold, probably hoping for a ransom: shipwrecked nobles were valuable.

latin: ET DUXIT EUM AD BELREM ET IBI EUM TENUIT
en: and took him to Beaurain and held him there
note: Harold is taken to Guy's castle at Beaurain.

latin: UBI HAROLD ⁊ WIDO PARABOLANT
en: Where Harold and Guy talk
note: The sign ⁊ is the medieval shorthand for 'and'. 'Parabolant' gives us French parler, 'to speak'.

latin: UBI NUNTII WILLELMI DUCIS VENERUNT AD WIDONE[M] · TUROLD
en: Where Duke William's messengers came to Guy · Turold
note: A small bearded man named Turold holds the horses. Nobody knows for certain who he was.

latin: NUNTII WILLELMI
en: William's messengers
note: William's men gallop to demand Harold's release.

latin: † HIC VENIT NUNTIUS AD WILGELMUM DUCEM
en: Here a messenger comes to Duke William
note: William, Duke of Normandy, hears the news of Harold's capture.

latin: HIC WIDO ADDUXIT HAROLDUM AD WILGELMUM NORMANNORUM DUCEM
en: Here Guy brought Harold to William, Duke of the Normans
note: Guy hands Harold over. William now has a powerful guest, and leverage.

latin: HIC DUX WILGELM[US] CUM HAROLDO VENIT AD PALATIU[M] SUU[M]
en: Here Duke William comes with Harold to his palace
note: They arrive at William's palace, probably at Rouen.

latin: UBI UNUS CLERICUS ET ÆLFGYVA [...]
en: Where a priest and Ælfgyva …
note: The tapestry's great mystery: the sentence has no verb, and nobody knows who Ælfgyva was or what scandal is hinted at. The naked figure in the border below suggests gossip.

latin: HIC WILLEM[US] DUX ET EXERCITUS EIUS VENERUNT AD MONTE[M] MICHAELIS
en: Here Duke William and his army came to Mont-Saint-Michel
note: William takes Harold on campaign against Brittany. Mont-Saint-Michel appears as a hill-top abbey.

latin: ET HIC TRANSIERUNT FLUMEN COSNONIS · HIC HAROLD DUX TRAHEBAT EOS DE ARENA
en: and here they crossed the river Couesnon · here Duke Harold pulled them out of the quicksand
note: Harold the hero rescues two Norman soldiers from the quicksand, one carried on his back.

latin: ET VENERUNT AD DOL ET CONAN FUGA VERTIT · REDNES
en: and they came to Dol, and Conan fled · Rennes
note: Duke Conan II of Brittany escapes from Dol by sliding down a rope.

latin: HIC MILITES WILLELMI DUCIS PUGNANT CONTRA DINANTES
en: Here Duke William's knights fight the people of Dinan
note: The Normans set fire to the wooden castle of Dinan.

latin: ET CUNAN CLAVES PORREXIT
en: and Conan handed over the keys
note: Conan surrenders, passing the keys of Dinan out on the tip of a lance.

latin: HIC WILLELM[US] DEDIT ARMA HAROLDO
en: Here William gave arms to Harold
note: William gives Harold weapons and armour, making him, in Norman eyes, William's man.

latin: HIE WILLELM[US] VENIT BAGIAS
en: Here William came to Bayeux
note: HIE is a stitching slip for HIC. Bayeux is the town where the tapestry was later kept.

latin: UBI HAROLD SACRAMENTUM FECIT WILLELMO DUCI
en: Where Harold swore an oath to Duke William
note: The most important scene for the Normans: Harold swears on holy relics, they said to support William's claim to the English throne.

latin: HIC HAROLD DUX REVERSUS EST AD ANGLICAM TERRAM
en: Here Duke Harold went back to England
note: Harold sails home. Faces watch from a building as he arrives.

latin: ET VENIT AD EDWARDU[M] REGEM
en: and he came to King Edward
note: Harold reports to Edward, who now looks old and frail and seems to scold him.

latin: HIC PORTATUR CORPUS EADWARDI REGIS AD ECCLESIAM S[AN]C[T]I PETRI AP[OSTO]LI
en: Here King Edward's body is carried to the Church of St Peter the Apostle
note: Edward's funeral at his new abbey, Westminster. A hand of God reaches down from heaven over the church.

latin: HIC EADWARDUS REX IN LECTO ALLOQUIT[UR] FIDELES
en: Here King Edward, in bed, speaks to his faithful followers
note: The story runs backwards here: Edward's deathbed comes after his funeral. English sources say he named Harold as his heir.

latin: ET HIC DEFUNCTUS EST
en: and here he died
note: Edward the Confessor dies, with no children.

latin: HIC DEDERUNT HAROLDO CORONA[M] REGIS
en: Here they gave Harold the king's crown
note: Harold is offered the crown the very next day.

latin: HIC RESIDET HAROLD REX ANGLORUM
en: Here sits Harold, King of the English
note: Harold II is crowned, probably at Westminster Abbey on the day of Edward's burial.

latin: STIGANT ARCHIEP[ISCOPU]S
en: Archbishop Stigand
note: Stigand, Archbishop of Canterbury, stands beside Harold. The Normans thought him an illegitimate archbishop, which made the coronation look shady.

latin: ISTI MIRANT[UR] STELLA[M]
en: These people marvel at the star
note: Halley's Comet blazes across the sky in late April 1066, seen as an omen of disaster.

latin: HAROLD
en: Harold
note: Harold listens to news while ghostly ships appear in the border below: an invasion is coming.

latin: HIC NAVIS ANGLICA VENIT IN TERRAM WILLELMI DUCIS
en: Here an English ship came to Duke William's land
note: News of Harold's coronation reaches Normandy.

latin: HIC WILLELM[US] DUX JUSSIT NAVES [A]EDIFICARE
en: Here Duke William ordered ships to be built
note: Trees are felled and planks shaped with axes and adzes: a whole fleet is built over the summer.

latin: HIC TRAHUNT NAVES AD MARE
en: Here they drag the ships to the sea
note: The new ships are hauled down to the water.

latin: ISTI PORTANT ARMAS AD NAVES ET HIC TRAHUNT CARRUM CUM VINO ET ARMIS
en: These men carry weapons to the ships, and here they pull a cart loaded with wine and weapons
note: Mail shirts, swords, helmets, and a barrel of wine: the essentials of an invasion.

latin: † HIC WILLELM[US] DUX IN MAGNO NAVIGIO MARE TRANSIVIT ET VENIT AD PEVENESÆ
en: Here Duke William crossed the sea in a great ship and came to Pevensey
note: The fleet crosses overnight and lands at Pevensey in Sussex, unopposed: Harold was in the north, fighting the Vikings.

latin: HIC EXEUNT CABALLI DE NAVIBUS
en: Here the horses get out of the ships
note: The Normans brought their warhorses across the Channel.

latin: ET HIC MILITES FESTINAVERUNT HESTINGA UT CIBUM RAPERENTUR
en: and here the knights hurried to Hastings to grab food
note: The invaders raid the countryside for supplies.

latin: HIC EST WADARD
en: This is Wadard
note: Wadard was a real Norman knight who later held lands in England from Bishop Odo.

latin: HIC COQUITUR CARO ET HIC MINISTRAVERUNT MINISTRI
en: Here the meat is cooked, and here the servants served it
note: A medieval cooking scene: kebabs on skewers, a pot over the fire, an oven.

latin: HIC FECERUN[T] PRANDIUM · ET HIC EPISCOPUS CIBU[M] ET POTU[M] BENEDICIT
en: Here they have a meal · and here the bishop blesses the food and drink
note: A feast that looks a little like the Last Supper, with Bishop Odo at the centre.

latin: ODO EP[ISCOPU]S WILLELM[US] ROTBERT
en: Bishop Odo, William, Robert
note: William sits between his two half-brothers, Odo of Bayeux and Robert of Mortain. Odo probably ordered the tapestry made.

latin: ISTE JUSSIT UT FODERETUR CASTELLUM AT HESTENGA · CEASTRA
en: He ordered a castle mound to be dug at Hastings · the camp
note: The English-style spellings AT and CEASTRA are clues that English embroiderers made the tapestry.

latin: HIC NUNTIATUM EST WILLELM[O] DE HAROLD[O]
en: Here William is told about Harold
note: A messenger brings news of Harold's army approaching.

latin: HIC DOMUS INCENDITUR
en: Here a house is burned
note: A woman and child flee a burning house, a rare glimpse of ordinary people in war.

latin: HIC MILITES EXIERUNT DE HESTENGA ET VENERUNT AD PR[O]ELIUM CONTRA HAROLDUM REGE[M]
en: Here the knights left Hastings and went to battle against King Harold
note: The Norman cavalry rides out on the morning of the battle.

latin: HIC WILLELM[US] DUX INTERROGAT VITAL[EM] SI VIDISSET HAROLDI EXERCITU[M]
en: Here Duke William asks Vital whether he has seen Harold's army
note: Vital, a scout, reports back. He too was a real tenant of Bishop Odo.

latin: ISTE NUNTIAT HAROLDUM REGE[M] DE EXERCITU WILLELMI DUCIS
en: This man tells King Harold about Duke William's army
note: An English lookout spots the Normans.

latin: HIC WILLELM[US] DUX ALLOQUITUR SUIS MILITIBUS UT PREPARAREN[T] SE VIRILITER ET SAPIENTER AD PR[O]ELIUM CONTRA ANGLORUM EXERCITU[M]
en: Here Duke William tells his knights to prepare bravely and wisely for battle against the English army
note: William's pre-battle speech. The long caption fills the space above the charging horsemen.

latin: HIC CECIDERUNT LEWINE ET GYRÐ FRATRES HAROLDI REGIS
en: Here fell Leofwine and Gyrth, King Harold's brothers
note: The English shield wall holds on the hill, but Harold's brothers are killed. The letter Ð (eth) is Old English.

latin: HIC CECIDERUNT SIMUL ANGLI ET FRANCI IN PR[O]ELIO
en: Here English and French fell together in battle
note: Horses tumble and men fall in a muddle at the foot of the hill.

latin: HIC ODO EP[ISCOPU]S BACULU[M] TENENS CONFORTAT PUEROS
en: Here Bishop Odo, holding a club, cheers on the young men
note: A bishop fighting? Odo carries a club, perhaps because clergy were not supposed to shed blood with a sword.

latin: HIC EST WILLEL[MUS] DUX
en: Here is Duke William
note: A rumour spread that William was dead, so he pushes back his helmet to show his face to his men.

latin: E[USTA]TIUS · HIC FRANCI PUGNANT ET CECIDERUNT QUI ERANT CUM HAROLDO
en: Eustace · here the French fight, and those who were with Harold fell
note: Count Eustace of Boulogne points to William. Harold's household troops die around him.

latin: HIC HAROLD REX INTERFECTUS EST
en: Here King Harold was killed
note: The famous scene. Whether Harold is the man with the arrow in his eye, the man cut down by a horseman, or both, is still argued about.

latin: ET FUGA VERTERUNT ANGLI
en: and the English turned and fled
note: The last surviving scene. The tapestry's true ending is lost, and these words may have been added by later restorers. William was crowned on Christmas Day 1066.
